title: Ezra 10:18–44
context: The chapter ends with a list of men found to have married foreign women, beginning with priests from the high priestly family and other priestly houses, then Levites, a singer, gatekeepers, and men of Israel grouped by family. The priests pledge to put away their wives and offer a ram for their guilt. Many of the lay family names also appear in the lists of returning exiles in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, such as Parosh, Pahathmoab, Elam, Zattu, Bebai, Bani, Harim, Hashum, and Nebo; the lists serve different purposes and are not harmonized here. The final verse notes that some of the men had children by these wives. The Hebrew of 10:44 is generally regarded as difficult, and translations render it in somewhat different ways.

verses.text: Among the sons of the priests there were found who had married foreign women: of the sons of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah.
verses.arminianNotes: Among the priests, sons of Jeshua son of Jozadak are named: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah. Arminian readers note that the list begins with the high priestly family, showing that the issue reached the community’s leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeshua son of Jozadak led the first return (Ezra 3:2), so the list does not spare prominent families. Both traditions read the verse as an honest record that includes those in positions of honor.

verses.text: They gave their hand that they would put away their wives; and being guilty, they offered a ram of the flock for their guilt.
verses.arminianNotes: These priests pledge to put away their wives and offer a ram for their guilt. Arminian readers note the public pledge and the guilt offering, which mark the priests’ acknowledgment of wrongdoing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the guilt offering as recalling the provisions of Leviticus 5:14–19. Shared ground: the verse reports the priests’ response as the narrator gives it, and both traditions read it without endorsement or polemic.

verses.text: Of the sons of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah. Arminian readers note that Immer is one of the priestly families listed among those who returned in Ezra 2:37, so the list follows established family lines.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the naming of each man as part of the record’s thoroughness. Both traditions read the verse as part of the list of priests, without drawing conclusions about the individuals beyond what is stated.

verses.text: Of the sons of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah. Arminian readers note that a priestly house named Harim appears in Ezra 2:39, and another Harim among the laity later in this list (10:31).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the list the reach of the problem across priestly families. Shared ground: the names are recorded as the text gives them, and both traditions read the verse as part of a sober historical register.

verses.text: Of the sons of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah. Arminian readers note that Pashhur is another priestly family from Ezra 2:38, and that six men are named from this house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the length of this entry as showing how widespread the issue was among the priests. Both traditions read the verse as historical record, without speculating about the circumstances of each marriage.

verses.text: Of the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer. Arminian readers note that Levites are included, as they were in the original report (9:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the detail of Kelaiah’s second name, which shows the care of the record. Shared ground: the verse lists Levites who were among those involved, and both traditions read it without further judgment.

verses.text: Of the singers: Eliashib. Of the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the singers: Eliashib; of the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri. Arminian readers note that temple servants of every kind are named, from musicians to those who kept the gates.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a family of gatekeepers named Shallum appears in Ezra 2:42, though a direct link is not certain. Both traditions read the verse as completing the list of temple personnel before turning to the laity.

verses.text: Of Israel: Of the sons of Parosh: Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malchijah, and Benaiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Of Israel, of the sons of Parosh: Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malchijah, and Benaiah. Arminian readers note that the list now turns to lay families, beginning with Parosh, the first family named in Ezra 2:3.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Malchijah appears twice, showing that names were often shared within a family group. Shared ground: both traditions read the lay section as following family lines known from the return lists.

verses.text: Of the sons of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah. Arminian readers note that Shecaniah, who first proposed the covenant, was of the sons of Elam (10:2), so his own family is listed here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of Shecaniah’s family as showing that the reform did not spare its own advocates. Both traditions read the verse with Ezra 2:7 in view, where Elam appears among the returning families.

verses.text: Of the sons of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza. Arminian readers note that Zattu appears in Ezra 2:8 among the families that returned, and that several names here recur elsewhere in the list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the recurrence of common names such as Mattaniah and Jeremoth as typical of the period. Shared ground: the list records these men by family, and both traditions read it without assigning individual motives.

verses.text: Of the sons of Bebai: Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Bebai: Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai. Arminian readers observe that this is one of the shorter lay entries; the family of Bebai is counted among the returnees at Ezra 2:11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the brief entry as part of a record that names people rather than summarizing them. Both traditions read the verse as historical register, honoring the text’s concern with accuracy rather than drawing lessons from each name.

verses.text: Of the sons of Bani: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Bani: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth. Arminian readers note that Bani appears in Ezra 2:10, while the parallel in Nehemiah 7:15 reads Binnui; the difference is noted, not harmonized.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a second “sons of Bani” heading appears in 10:34, and the repetition is discussed by interpreters. Shared ground: both traditions read the entry as recorded and leave the repeated name unresolved.

verses.text: Of the sons of Pahathmoab: Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Pahathmoab: Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh. Arminian readers note that Pahathmoab is a large family in Ezra 2:6, and eight men are named here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the names Bezalel and Manasseh, which echo earlier figures in Israel’s history. Both traditions read the verse as part of the record, without attaching symbolic meaning to the names.

verses.text: Of the sons of Harim: Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Shimeon,
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Harim: Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Shimeon. Arminian readers note that this Harim is a lay family (compare Ezra 2:32), distinct from the priestly Harim in 10:21.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the distinction between the two families named Harim as an example of the list’s careful organization. Shared ground: the entry continues into the next verse, and both traditions read it simply as part of the register.

verses.text: Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah.
verses.arminianNotes: Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah complete the sons of Harim. Arminian readers note that the name Benjamin is used here as a personal name, not the tribe, a reminder of how tribal names could be given to individuals.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completion of this entry as part of the list’s steady progression through the families. Both traditions read the verse as a continuation of 10:31, without further comment on the individuals.

verses.text: Of the sons of Hashum: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Hashum: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei. Arminian readers note that Hashum appears in Ezra 2:19 among the returning families, and seven men are listed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how the list repeatedly names Manasseh and Shimei in different families. Shared ground: both traditions read the entry as part of a careful record of the community, rather than as commentary on any particular man.

verses.text: Of the sons of Bani: Maadai, Amram, Uel,
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Bani: Maadai, Amram, Uel. Arminian readers note that this second heading for Bani begins the longest single entry, running through 10:42, and that the repetition of the family name is not explained.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some suggest a different family name may originally have stood here, but the WEB reads Bani, and the question is left open. Both traditions read the entry as recorded without resolving the repetition.

verses.text: Benaiah, Bedeiah, Cheluhi,
verses.arminianNotes: Benaiah, Bedeiah, and Cheluhi continue the list. Arminian readers note that the names keep coming in groups of three, a pattern in this part of the list that gives it a steady rhythm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the length of this family’s entry a sign of how many households were affected. Shared ground: the verse is a simple list of names, and both traditions read it as a continuation of the record begun in 10:34.

verses.text: Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib,
verses.arminianNotes: Vaniah, Meremoth, and Eliashib are named. Arminian readers note that names such as Meremoth and Eliashib also appear elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah, though these may be different people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers caution against identifying individuals across texts simply by shared names. Both traditions read the verse as part of the register, treating each name as recorded without speculative links.

verses.text: Mattaniah, Mattenai, Jaasu,
verses.arminianNotes: Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasu are named. Arminian readers note that similar names, such as Mattaniah and Mattenai, appear close together, reflecting common naming patterns built on the theme of gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the names as reminders of a community whose names often expressed faith in God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse simply as part of the list, without drawing theological conclusions from the names.

verses.text: Bani, Binnui, Shimei,
verses.arminianNotes: Bani, Binnui, and Shimei are named. Arminian readers note that Bani and Binnui appear here as personal names within the list, which may relate to the variation between Ezra 2:10 and Nehemiah 7:15.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the relationship between these names is uncertain and best left unresolved. Both traditions read the verse as recorded, acknowledging the complexity of the lists without forcing a harmonization.

verses.text: Shelemiah, Nathan, Adaiah,
verses.arminianNotes: Shelemiah, Nathan, and Adaiah are named. Arminian readers note that ordinary families from every part of the community appear in this register, not only leaders or priests.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as testimony that the whole community took part in the crisis and its resolution. Shared ground: the verse continues the record, and both traditions read it without further comment on the individuals.

verses.text: Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai,
verses.arminianNotes: Machnadebai, Shashai, and Sharai are named. Arminian readers note that several names in this section are unusual and appear only here, preserved in the record of the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the preservation of such rare names as part of the text’s commitment to an exact register. Both traditions read the verse simply as part of the list, without speculating about the meaning or origin of the names.

verses.text: Azarel, Shelemiah, Shemariah,
verses.arminianNotes: Azarel, Shelemiah, and Shemariah are named. Arminian readers note that Shelemiah appears a second time in this entry, showing that the same name could be borne by more than one man in a family group.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated names as reflecting the common naming customs of the period. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the register, without assuming any connection beyond what the text states.

verses.text: Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph.
verses.arminianNotes: Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph complete the long entry for the sons of Bani. Arminian readers note that the family contributes many names, more than any other group in the list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the conclusion of this entry as bringing the record near its end. Both traditions read the verse as the last part of the Bani entry begun in 10:34, recorded without further evaluation.

verses.text: Of the sons of Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Iddo, Joel, and Benaiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the sons of Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Iddo, Joel, and Benaiah. Arminian readers note that Nebo appears in Ezra 2:29 as a place-based group among the returnees, and it closes the list of families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the final family entry as completing a register that covers priests, Levites, temple servants, and laity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the record, closing the lists before the final summary.

verses.text: All these had taken foreign wives. Some of them had wives by whom they had children.
verses.arminianNotes: All these had taken foreign wives, and some had wives by whom they had children. Arminian readers note that the book ends on this sober note, without describing what became of the women and children.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Hebrew of this verse is generally regarded as difficult, and translations differ somewhat. Shared ground: both traditions read the ending soberly; many also read it alongside other texts such as Ruth and Nehemiah 13:23–27.
